halal_clear.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
halal_clear.names-value: All ingredients on this product's label were scanned by BOTIA's classification engine.
halal_clear.aliases-value: No Haram or Mashbooh ingredients detected in this label.
halal_clear.description: BOTIA scanned the full ingredient list of this product and found no ingredients classified as Haram (forbidden) or Mashbooh (doubtful) in its database.
halal_clear.uses-value: No pork derivatives, no alcohol, no undeclared animal-derived emulsifiers, no insect-derived colorants, and no other flagged ingredients were found on this label.
halal_clear.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
halal_clear.plain-explanation: Based on what is declared on the label, this product does not contain ingredients that BOTIA classifies as Haram or doubtful. This is a positive result — but it comes with important limits.
halal_clear.everyday-value: The label looks clean according to BOTIA's current database. This is good information — but not a Halal certification.
halal_clear.why-explanation: BOTIA shows the Halal Clear icon when its engine finds no flagged ingredients in the scanned label. This reflects what is visible and declared on the label — not what may be undeclared or present through cross-contamination.
halal_clear.display-logic: No Haram or Mashbooh ingredients detected on label → Halal Clear classification
halal_clear.can-1: Pork and pork derivatives (gelatin, lard, collagen, bacon, ham)
halal_clear.can-2: Alcohol and alcohol-derived ingredients (ethanol, wine extract, beer extract)
halal_clear.can-4: Fat-derived emulsifiers with undeclared animal origin (E471, E472, E481, E482, E475)
halal_clear.can-6: Cheese and rennet with undeclared origin
halal_clear.can-9: Wine vinegar, malt extract, hop extract with uncertain processing
halal_clear.cannot-1: That the product is certified Halal — only a certification body can do that
halal_clear.cannot-2: That there is no cross-contamination in shared production facilities
halal_clear.cannot-3: That ingredients not yet in BOTIA's database are Halal
halal_clear.cannot-4: That processing aids not listed on the label are Halal
halal_clear.cannot-5: That the slaughter method of any animal-derived ingredient meets Halal requirements
halal_clear.cannot-note: BOTIA reads declared ingredients. For full Halal assurance, look for a certified Halal logo from a recognised certification body.
halal_clear.sources-items: Recognised Halal certification logos: HFC (Halal Food Council Europe) · IFANCA · JAKIM (Malaysia) · MUI (Indonesia) · ESMA (UAE) · HCB (Halal Certification Body Netherlands)

alcohol.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
alcohol.names-value: Ethanol, Ethyl alcohol, Wine, Beer, Spirits, Wine extract, Beer extract
alcohol.description: Alcohol (ethanol) is used in food as a solvent, preservative, or flavouring carrier. It appears directly as wine, beer, or spirits, or hidden inside extracts and alcoholic flavourings. BOTIA classifies this ingredient as Haram when the alcoholic origin is clear and direct.
alcohol.uses-value: Chocolates with liqueur, alcoholic sauces, marinades with wine or beer, alcoholic flavourings in confectionery
alcohol.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
alcohol.plain-explanation: Ethanol is a psychoactive substance produced by fermentation. In Islamic dietary law, any amount of intentionally added ethanol renders a product Haram — not just products that cause intoxication. The prohibition applies when the alcoholic origin is clear and direct.
alcohol.everyday-value: A sauce listing 'wine extract' or 'beer extract' is Haram. No ambiguity.
alcohol.why-explanation: BOTIA detected a clearly alcohol-derived ingredient on this product's label. The alcoholic origin is direct and unambiguous.
alcohol.display-logic: Clear alcohol or alcoholic extract detected on label → Haram classification
alcohol.can-1: Ethanol and ethyl alcohol listed directly
alcohol.can-2: Wine, beer, spirits listed as ingredients
alcohol.can-4: Alcoholic flavourings where alcohol is the declared carrier
alcohol.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
alcohol.cannot-2: Detect alcohol that evaporated during cooking
alcohol.cannot-3: Assess whether processing alcohol was fully removed
alcohol.cannot-note: Note: wine vinegar, malt extract, and hop extract are handled separately under Doubt/Mashbooh, as their permissibility depends on origin and processing method.
alcohol.sources-items: IFANCA · ESMA UAE Halal Standard · EFSA

pork_gelatin.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
pork_gelatin.names-value: Pork gelatin, Lard, Pork fat, Bacon, Ham, Pork collagen, Pork liver
pork_gelatin.description: Pork and its derivatives appear in many processed foods, often in unexpected places. Gelatin is widely used as a gelling agent in sweets, yoghurts, and capsules. Lard is used in pastry and fried products.
pork_gelatin.uses-value: Gummy sweets, marshmallows, yoghurt, pâtés, sausages, some pastries, stock cubes, medication capsules
pork_gelatin.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
pork_gelatin.plain-explanation: Pork and all its derivatives are Haram in Islamic dietary law. This includes gelatin, lard, collagen, and any flavouring or additive derived from pig. The prohibition applies regardless of quantity.
pork_gelatin.everyday-value: Gummy bears often contain pork gelatin. Gelatin without a certified Halal or plant-based source label is suspicious.
pork_gelatin.why-explanation: BOTIA detected pork or a pork-derived ingredient on this product's label. This is an unconditional Haram classification.
pork_gelatin.display-logic: Pork or pork derivative detected on label → Haram classification
pork_gelatin.can-1: Pork, bacon, ham, lard explicitly listed
pork_gelatin.can-2: Pork gelatin when source is specified on label
pork_gelatin.can-3: Pork liver, pork fat, pork collagen
pork_gelatin.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
pork_gelatin.cannot-2: Detect cross-contamination in shared production facilities
pork_gelatin.cannot-3: Identify gelatin when the source is not declared on label — see Doubt
pork_gelatin.cannot-note: BOTIA reads what is on the label. Undeclared gelatin source is classified separately under Doubt/Mashbooh.
pork_gelatin.sources-items: IFANCA · JAKIM Malaysia Halal Standard · EU Food Information Regulation (FIR) 1169/2011

carmine_e120.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
carmine_e120.names-value: E120, Carmine, Carminic acid, Cochineal extract, Natural Red 4
carmine_e120.description: E120 is a red colorant derived from the dried bodies of the cochineal insect (Dactylopius coccus). It is used to give pink, red, and purple colours to food and drinks.
carmine_e120.uses-value: Yoghurts, fruit juices, sweets, ice cream, jams, some meat products
carmine_e120.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
carmine_e120.plain-explanation: Carmine is made from crushed insects. Most Islamic scholars classify insect-derived ingredients as Haram. BOTIA classifies E120 as Haram following the majority Hanafi, Maliki, and Shafi'i scholarly positions.
carmine_e120.everyday-value: That pink strawberry yoghurt may be red because of crushed insects.
carmine_e120.why-explanation: BOTIA detected E120 / Carmine on this product's label. This colorant is derived from insects, which are not permissible under the majority scholarly position.
carmine_e120.display-logic: Insect-derived colorant detected → Haram classification (majority scholarly position)
carmine_e120.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
carmine_e120.cannot-2: Reflect minority scholarly positions that permit some insect derivatives
carmine_e120.cannot-3: Detect carmine used in processing aids not listed on label
carmine_e120.cannot-note: Scholarly opinion on insects varies between madhabs. BOTIA follows the majority position. Your religious authority may differ.
carmine_e120.sources-items: EFSA E120 assessment · IFANCA · Islamic Food Council of Europe (IFCE) · EU Regulation 1333/2008

e471.ingredient-name: E471 — Mono- and Diglycerides of Fatty Acids
e471.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
e471.names-value: E471, Mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids, Glycerol monostearate, Glycerol monopalmitate
e471.description: E471 is one of the most common food emulsifiers. It is used to blend water and fat together, improving texture in baked goods, margarine, ice cream, and processed foods. It can be derived from animal fat (including pork), vegetable oils, or synthetic sources.
e471.uses-value: Bread, cakes, margarine, ice cream, chocolate, instant noodles, processed cheese, ready meals
e471.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
e471.plain-explanation: E471 is a fat-derived emulsifier. The problem is that European food labelling law does not require manufacturers to declare whether it comes from animal or vegetable sources. You see 'E471' on the label — but not where it came from.
e471.everyday-value: The bread you buy every day probably contains E471. Whether it is Halal depends on the source — which the label does not tell you.
e471.why-explanation: BOTIA detected E471 on this label. Because the origin (animal or vegetable) cannot be determined from the label alone, BOTIA classifies this as Mashbooh — doubtful.
e471.display-logic: Origin unknown from label → Mashbooh classification
e471.can-2: Mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids listed by name
e471.can-4: Emulsifier E471 in any position on the ingredient list
e471.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
e471.cannot-2: Determine whether this E471 is animal or vegetable derived
e471.cannot-3: Access manufacturer sourcing data not on the label
e471.cannot-note: To confirm Halal status, look for a certified Halal logo on the packaging, or contact the manufacturer directly.
e471.sources-items: EFSA E471 assessment · EU Regulation 1333/2008 · IFANCA · European Halal Certification Institute (EHCI)

e481.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
e481.description: E481 is an emulsifier and dough conditioner widely used in baked goods. It improves volume and softness in bread and extends shelf life. It is produced from stearic acid (which can be animal or vegetable derived) and lactic acid.
e481.uses-value: Bread, rolls, cakes, biscuits, waffles, pancake mixes, some dairy products
e481.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
e481.plain-explanation: E481 contains stearic acid, which can come from animal fat (including pork fat) or from vegetable oils. The label does not specify the source. This uncertainty makes it Mashbooh.
e481.everyday-value: That soft supermarket bread stays soft thanks to E481. Its Halal status depends on where the stearic acid came from — unknown from the label.
e481.why-explanation: BOTIA detected E481 on this label. The stearic acid component can be animal or vegetable derived, and the label does not declare the source.
e481.display-logic: Animal or vegetable origin undeclared → Mashbooh classification
e481.can-4: Emulsifier E481 in any position on the ingredient list
e481.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
e481.cannot-2: Determine the animal or vegetable origin of the stearic acid
e481.cannot-3: Access supplier chain data not on the label
e481.cannot-note: Look for a Halal certification logo or contact the manufacturer to confirm stearic acid origin.
e481.sources-items: EFSA E481 assessment · EU Regulation 1333/2008 · IFANCA

e482.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
e482.description: E482 is the calcium salt version of E481. It functions similarly as a dough conditioner and emulsifier. Like E481, it contains stearic acid of potentially animal or vegetable origin.
e482.uses-value: Bread, pastry, biscuits, cake mixes, some pasta products
e482.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
e482.plain-explanation: E482 has the same origin uncertainty as E481. The stearic acid component may come from animal fat or vegetable oil. The label does not tell you which.
e482.everyday-value: Same doubt as E481 — the source of the fat component is not declared.
e482.why-explanation: BOTIA detected E482 on this label. Origin of the stearic acid component is undeclared, making this Mashbooh.
e482.display-logic: Animal or vegetable origin undeclared → Mashbooh classification
e482.can-4: Emulsifier E482 in any position on the ingredient list
e482.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
e482.cannot-2: Determine the origin of the stearic acid
e482.cannot-note: Look for a Halal certification logo or contact the manufacturer.
e482.sources-items: EFSA E482 assessment · EU Regulation 1333/2008 · IFANCA

e472.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
e472.names-value: E472a, E472b, E472c, E472d, E472e, E472f — Esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
e472.aliases-value: Acetic acid esters, Lactic acid esters, Citric acid esters, DATEM, PGMS
e472.description: The E472 family covers several esters of fatty acids used as emulsifiers and stabilisers. Like E471, they can be derived from animal or vegetable fats. The label rarely specifies the source.
e472.uses-value: Bread, cakes, whipped creams, margarine, coffee whiteners, processed meats
e472.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
e472.plain-explanation: The E472 group has the same core problem as E471: the fat source (animal or vegetable) is not declared on the label. Any variant in this group is Mashbooh until confirmed.
e472.everyday-value: E472e (DATEM) is very common in industrial bread. Its Halal status depends on fat origin — undeclared.
e472.why-explanation: BOTIA detected an E472 variant on this label. Fat origin undeclared → Mashbooh.
e472.can-1: Any E472 variant (E472a through E472f) listed by number
e472.can-2: DATEM (diacetyl tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides)
e472.can-3: Lactic acid esters of fatty acids
e472.can-4: Citric acid esters of fatty acids
e472.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
e472.cannot-2: Determine animal or vegetable origin of the fat component
e472.cannot-3: Distinguish between E472 variants in terms of risk
e472.cannot-note: All E472 variants carry the same origin uncertainty. Confirm with manufacturer or look for Halal certification.
e472.sources-items: EFSA E472 assessment · EU Regulation 1333/2008 · IFANCA

e475.ingredient-name: E475 — Polyglycerol Esters of Fatty Acids
e475.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
e475.names-value: E475, Polyglycerol esters of fatty acids, PGE
e475.aliases-value: Polyglycerol fatty acid esters, Emulsifier E475
e475.description: E475 is an emulsifier used in baked goods, confectionery, and low-fat spreads. It is made from glycerol and fatty acids. Both components can be animal or vegetable derived.
e475.uses-value: Cakes, biscuits, chocolate, low-fat spreads, some ice creams
e475.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
e475.plain-explanation: E475 is another fat-derived emulsifier where the source is not declared on the label. Same uncertainty as E471 and E472.
e475.everyday-value: Common in industrial cakes and chocolate. Origin not declared.
e475.why-explanation: BOTIA detected E475 on this label. Animal or vegetable origin undeclared → Mashbooh.
e475.can-2: Polyglycerol esters of fatty acids listed by name
e475.can-4: Emulsifier E475 in any position on the ingredient list
e475.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
e475.cannot-2: Determine the origin of the fatty acid component
e475.cannot-note: Confirm with manufacturer or look for Halal certification logo.
e475.sources-items: EFSA E475 assessment · EU Regulation 1333/2008 · IFANCA

natural_aroma.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
natural_aroma.names-value: Natural flavouring, Natural flavour, Natural aroma, Aroma naturel
natural_aroma.description: Natural flavourings can be derived from plants, animals, microorganisms, or fermentation. EU law requires declaring them as 'natural flavouring' but does not require declaring the source. They may contain alcohol as a solvent or carrier.
natural_aroma.uses-value: Almost all processed foods: snacks, drinks, dairy, confectionery, sauces, ready meals
natural_aroma.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
natural_aroma.plain-explanation: 'Natural' does not mean plant-based or Halal. A natural flavouring can come from any animal, including pork. It can also use alcohol as a carrier solvent. The label tells you nothing about the source.
natural_aroma.everyday-value: Vanilla flavouring labelled 'natural' may be fine — or it may contain animal extracts or alcohol as carrier. There is no way to tell from the label.
natural_aroma.why-explanation: BOTIA detected natural flavouring on this label. The source and carrier are undeclared. This is one of the most common hidden uncertainty points in processed food.
natural_aroma.display-logic: Source and carrier undeclared → Mashbooh classification
natural_aroma.can-1: Natural flavouring / natural flavour listed in any language
natural_aroma.can-2: Aroma naturel, natürliches Aroma, aroma natural
natural_aroma.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
natural_aroma.cannot-2: Determine whether the flavouring is plant, animal, or fermentation derived
natural_aroma.cannot-3: Detect whether alcohol is used as the carrier solvent
natural_aroma.cannot-note: This is one of the most opaque ingredients in food labelling. Only certified Halal products guarantee the flavouring source.
natural_aroma.sources-items: EU Regulation 1334/2008 on flavourings · EFSA flavourings opinion · IFANCA · EHCI

cheese_rennet.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
cheese_rennet.aliases-value: Animal rennet, Chymosin, Microbial rennet (when unspecified), Fromage, Queso
cheese_rennet.description: Rennet is the enzyme used to coagulate milk into cheese. Traditional rennet comes from the stomach lining of slaughtered calves (animal rennet). Modern cheese may use microbial rennet, fermentation-produced chymosin (FPC), or plant rennet — all potentially Halal. The label rarely specifies which.
cheese_rennet.uses-value: All hard and semi-hard cheeses, cheese powder in snacks and sauces, processed cheese products
cheese_rennet.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
cheese_rennet.plain-explanation: Cheese contains rennet. If the rennet is from a non-Halal slaughtered animal, the cheese is Haram. If it is microbial or plant-based, it may be Halal. The label almost never tells you which type was used.
cheese_rennet.everyday-value: Parmesan, Grana Padano, Manchego — all use animal rennet by law or tradition. Most supermarket cheddar does not specify.
cheese_rennet.why-explanation: BOTIA detected cheese or rennet on this label without a Halal certification. The rennet source is undeclared → Mashbooh.
cheese_rennet.can-2: Rennet or coagulant listed without source specification
cheese_rennet.can-4: Chymosin when source is not specified
cheese_rennet.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
cheese_rennet.cannot-2: Determine whether the rennet is animal, microbial, or plant-based
cheese_rennet.cannot-3: Assess the slaughter method of animals used for rennet
cheese_rennet.cannot-note: Vegetarian cheese logos indicate non-animal rennet. Halal logos confirm the full production chain.
cheese_rennet.sources-items: EU FIR 1169/2011 · EFSA · IFANCA · Islamic Food Council of Europe

enzymes.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
enzymes.aliases-value: Amylase, Lipase, Protease, Lactase (when source unspecified)
enzymes.description: Enzymes are used in food production to improve texture, flavour, and shelf life. They can come from animal organs (including pork pancreas for lipase), bacteria, fungi, or genetic engineering. EU law does not require declaring the source on the consumer label.
enzymes.uses-value: Bread, cheese, beer, fruit juices, starch-based products, dairy
enzymes.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
enzymes.plain-explanation: The word 'enzymes' on a label hides a wide range of possible sources. Lipase from pork pancreas is commonly used in cheese production. Without source declaration, there is no way to know.
enzymes.everyday-value: Enzymes in bread are usually fungal — probably fine. Enzymes in cheese are high risk without certification.
enzymes.why-explanation: BOTIA detected enzymes on this label without source specification. Animal origin cannot be excluded → Mashbooh.
enzymes.can-1: Enzymes or enzyme listed on ingredient list
enzymes.can-2: Specific enzyme names without source (amylase, lipase, protease)
enzymes.can-4: Lactase and other dairy-related enzymes without source
enzymes.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
enzymes.cannot-2: Determine whether the enzyme is animal, microbial, or plant derived
enzymes.cannot-3: Identify processing aids used but not listed on label
enzymes.cannot-note: Halal certification is the only reliable way to confirm enzyme sources in processed food.
enzymes.sources-items: EU Regulation 1332/2008 on food enzymes · EFSA · IFANCA · EHCI

gelatin.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
gelatin.aliases-value: Beef gelatin (when undeclared), Fish gelatin (when undeclared), Collagen peptides
gelatin.description: Gelatin is a protein derived from animal skin, bones, and connective tissue. It can come from pork (Haram), cattle (Halal if properly slaughtered), or fish (generally Halal). When the label just says 'gelatin' without specifying the source, the origin is unknown.
gelatin.uses-value: Gummy sweets, marshmallows, yoghurt, jelly, ice cream, some medications and supplements
gelatin.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
gelatin.plain-explanation: Gelatin without a source declaration is one of the most common hidden risks in processed food. Pork gelatin is widely used because it is cheaper. Without a Halal logo, there is no guarantee.
gelatin.everyday-value: If the label says 'gelatin' and there is no Halal logo, assume pork until confirmed otherwise.
gelatin.why-explanation: BOTIA detected gelatin on this label without a source declaration. Pork origin cannot be excluded → Mashbooh.
gelatin.can-1: Gelatin or gelatine listed without source
gelatin.can-4: Gelatin in compound ingredients (e.g. 'yoghurt coating (contains gelatin)')
gelatin.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
gelatin.cannot-2: Determine whether gelatin is from pork, beef, or fish
gelatin.cannot-3: Confirm slaughter method for beef or fish gelatin
gelatin.cannot-note: Pork gelatin is classified as Haram (see Haram section). This card applies when the source is undeclared.

whey_powder.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
whey_powder.names-value: Whey powder, Whey protein, Dried whey, Whey solids
whey_powder.aliases-value: Sweet whey, Acid whey, Whey permeate, Milk whey
whey_powder.description: Whey is a by-product of cheese making. The concern for Halal is that the cheese process uses rennet — which may be from non-Halal slaughtered animals. Whey powder may also undergo processing steps involving animal-derived enzymes.
whey_powder.uses-value: Protein supplements, sports nutrition, biscuits, bread, processed foods, baby formula
whey_powder.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
whey_powder.plain-explanation: Whey itself is dairy — not inherently Haram. The doubt comes from the cheese-making process it derives from: if the rennet used was from a non-Halal slaughtered animal, the whey carries that doubt.
whey_powder.everyday-value: Whey protein powder is very common in sports nutrition. Without Halal certification, the rennet chain is unknown.
whey_powder.why-explanation: BOTIA detected whey powder on this label. The rennet origin in the cheese production process is undeclared → Mashbooh.
whey_powder.display-logic: Rennet origin in production chain undeclared → Mashbooh classification
whey_powder.can-1: Whey powder, whey protein, dried whey
whey_powder.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
whey_powder.cannot-2: Trace the rennet used in the originating cheese process
whey_powder.cannot-3: Confirm the enzyme chain in whey processing
whey_powder.cannot-note: Halal-certified whey products exist. Look for the certification logo, especially in sports nutrition.
whey_powder.sources-items: EU FIR 1169/2011 · IFANCA · EHCI · Codex Alimentarius

lactic_acid.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
lactic_acid.names-value: Lactic acid, E270, Lactate, Sodium lactate (E325), Potassium lactate (E326)
lactic_acid.aliases-value: L-lactic acid, DL-lactic acid, Fermentation lactic acid
lactic_acid.description: Lactic acid is a natural acid produced by fermentation. It can be derived from plant sugars (corn, beet, sugarcane) or from dairy (lactose fermentation) or animal muscle tissue. The production method determines its Halal status.
lactic_acid.uses-value: Bread, pickled products, dairy, meat products, salad dressings, beverages, confectionery
lactic_acid.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
lactic_acid.plain-explanation: Most commercial lactic acid is plant-derived today — but this is not always declared. When derived from dairy or animal sources, it carries additional doubt for some scholars. The label does not specify origin.
lactic_acid.everyday-value: Lactic acid in bread is almost always plant-derived fermentation. In meat products, the source is less clear.
lactic_acid.why-explanation: BOTIA detected lactic acid on this label. The production source is not declared → Mashbooh by precaution.
lactic_acid.can-1: Lactic acid and E270 listed directly
lactic_acid.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
lactic_acid.cannot-2: Determine plant, dairy, or animal origin of lactic acid
lactic_acid.cannot-3: Access fermentation substrate data not on label
lactic_acid.cannot-note: In practice, most lactic acid is plant-derived. Precautionary classification as Mashbooh reflects the lack of declaration.
lactic_acid.sources-items: EFSA E270 assessment · EU Regulation 1333/2008 · IFANCA

wine_vinegar.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
wine_vinegar.names-value: Wine vinegar, Red wine vinegar, White wine vinegar, Balsamic vinegar, Sherry vinegar
wine_vinegar.aliases-value: Vinaigre de vin, Weinessig, Azijn (wine-based), Aceto balsamico
wine_vinegar.description: Wine vinegar is produced by fermenting wine into acetic acid. During complete fermentation, ethanol converts to acetic acid. The question for Halal is whether the transformation is complete and whether any residual alcohol remains. Scholarly positions differ significantly.
wine_vinegar.uses-value: Salad dressings, marinades, sauces, pickles, condiments, balsamic glazes
wine_vinegar.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
wine_vinegar.plain-explanation: Wine vinegar starts as wine (Haram) and transforms through fermentation. Most Islamic scholars agree that fully transformed vinegar is permissible — but there is debate about whether commercial wine vinegar is always fully transformed, and about whether the wine origin itself matters.
wine_vinegar.everyday-value: Balsamic vinegar of Modena, red wine vinegar in salad dressings — common in European cooking. Many Muslim scholars permit it. Others do not. BOTIA flags it as a decision point.
wine_vinegar.why-explanation: BOTIA detected wine vinegar on this label. Scholarly opinion on wine vinegar is divided. BOTIA classifies it as Mashbooh so you can make an informed decision based on your own religious authority.
wine_vinegar.display-logic: Scholarly disagreement on wine-origin vinegar → Mashbooh classification
wine_vinegar.can-3: Red wine vinegar and white wine vinegar
wine_vinegar.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
wine_vinegar.cannot-2: Verify that fermentation was complete and no residual alcohol remains
wine_vinegar.cannot-3: Reflect your specific madhab position on wine vinegar
wine_vinegar.cannot-note: Many Halal certification bodies permit wine vinegar. Others do not. Check your trusted religious authority.
wine_vinegar.sources-items: IFANCA position on vinegar · Islamic Food Council of Europe · Codex Alimentarius · ESMA UAE Halal Standard

malt_extract.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
malt_extract.names-value: Malt extract, Barley malt extract, Malt syrup, Malted barley
malt_extract.aliases-value: Mout extract, Gerstenmalzextrakt, Extrait de malt
malt_extract.description: Malt extract is derived from germinated barley. In its pure form it contains no alcohol and is generally considered permissible. However, malt extract can also be a by-product of beer brewing — in which case it may retain traces of alcohol or have been produced in shared facilities with alcoholic products.
malt_extract.uses-value: Bread, breakfast cereals, biscuits, malted drinks, chocolate, some confectionery
malt_extract.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
malt_extract.plain-explanation: Pure malt extract from germinated grain is fine. Malt extract from beer production is uncertain. The label does not specify which process was used.
malt_extract.everyday-value: Malt extract in breakfast cereal is almost certainly from grain, not beer. In a craft sauce or flavouring, less certain.
malt_extract.why-explanation: BOTIA detected malt extract on this label. The production process (grain-only vs beer by-product) is undeclared → Mashbooh by precaution.
malt_extract.display-logic: Production process and potential alcohol contact undeclared → Mashbooh classification
malt_extract.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision

hop_extract.subtitle: A BOTIA Translation · Understanding Food Labels
hop_extract.names-value: Hop extract, Hops extract, Humulus lupulus extract
hop_extract.description: Hop extract is derived from the hop plant (Humulus lupulus). Hops are primarily associated with beer production and are used as a bittering and flavouring agent. Hop extract can be obtained using alcohol (ethanol) as the extraction solvent — meaning the final extract may contain residual alcohol.
hop_extract.uses-value: Flavourings, some bread and baked goods, herbal products, non-alcoholic beer, health supplements
hop_extract.section-what-means: What It Means in Plain Language
hop_extract.plain-explanation: Hop extract is not always alcohol-extracted. But when it is, and when residual alcohol remains in the final product, it becomes problematic. The label does not declare the extraction method.
hop_extract.everyday-value: Hop extract in a flavouring or supplement — the extraction solvent is almost never declared.
hop_extract.why-explanation: BOTIA detected hop extract on this label. The extraction solvent is undeclared, and alcohol extraction is common in hop processing → Mashbooh.
hop_extract.display-logic: Extraction solvent undeclared — alcohol extraction possible → Mashbooh classification
hop_extract.can-2: Hops extract and Humulus lupulus extract
hop_extract.can-4: Hop flavouring when source is hops
hop_extract.cannot-1: Tell you what to eat or avoid — that is your decision
hop_extract.cannot-2: Determine whether CO2 or alcohol was used as extraction solvent
hop_extract.cannot-3: Measure residual alcohol in the final extract
hop_extract.cannot-note: CO2-extracted hop extract carries no alcohol concern. Alcohol-extracted versions do. Without declaration, BOTIA applies precautionary classification.
